problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is $(t+1)\,m/s,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=2\,s$ and $t=4\,s.$

feedback.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ when $t=0\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=4\,s.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{t}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
2=\sqrt{0}+0+C\,⟹\,C=2.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\sqrt{t}+t+2.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1,$ is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=\sqrt{1}+1+2=4\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=4$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(4)=\sqrt{4}+4+2=8\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {8}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {4}^{2} \\  & =192-48 \\  & =144\,J.\end{aligned}
$$
